review:
[h1] So... The Original Fallout. [/h1]

I have put a Pros/Cons section at the foot of this review, for those not fond of reading.

You know... You know how games used to be good right? [i] When less was better? [/i] You know what I mean: like in old horror games when the controls were so terrible that it added to fear factor. Well, this game at first glance is pretty standard. I bought the classics bundle because I admit... I had never played the original fallouts before falling in love with Fallout 3 and New Vegas. I wanted to see where these games originated. 

I played the game for half an hour... I despised it. Absolutely hated it. [strike] I quickly became incredibly butthurt [/strike] I had issues with the controls, having not been too well acquainted with turn based titles before this point. 

The urge came many months later to retry the game, I thoroughly enjoyed playing for the next 28 hours (I had breaks of course, like... come on). This was a very, very sloppy playthrough. But trudging through the wastelands clinging to dear life... I still had a hell of a time. Anyway, this playthrough ended at the 28 hours (in which I didn't have much to show for, having messed around the whole time) because I half a**ed the 'ending' and left it sat for maybe a couple years?

This is when we come to the present. Fallout has ruined my social life this past week... [spoiler] think it was just the past two days. [/spoiler] I was oblivious to the outside world the whole time while playing, as if I was temporarily brainwashed. I put in 34 hours to be graced with the end of the game. Also, just finished it about an hour ago, thought I'd write this while I was still in awe. 

A couple indicators that lead me to believe this playthrough was more successful was: levelling had got me 75HP (Health Points), the Dweller brandished high tech weaponary capable of dealing up to around 450 damage, an untouchable set of T-51b Power Armour and... 63,000 caps. All this could be your's for the low, low price of: [spoiler] [your social life]. [/spoiler] You'd expect to have this equipment depending on character build by the end of the game. Well, maybe not the caps - spent too much time earning caps I'd never use. Out of curiosity, once I got there I had a look at the bad ending. I felt so accountable for the events that transpired in game following this that I was actually sorry... until I reloaded a save and completed the game the way I originally intended. 

Everyone lived happily ever after. Apart from... [spoiler] The Followers of the Apocalypse, The Supermutants/Nightkin, The Regulators, The Children of the Cathedral, The Raiders, of course the many dead and even the Vault Dweller... Now that I think of it, I lied. [/spoiler]

With most games, spending 34 hours would be reflected upon as a waste but I found it completely worthwhile, if even it was only to learn about the early fallout story. It will at least teach you one thing: to wish luck on anyone who survives complete nuclear world annihilation, cause that'll be the easy part.

-Original and sharp humour balanced 
perfectly with the feeling of dread

-"Maximum Blood"

[h1] Cons: [/h1]

minor changes, ability to 'push companions' - see
the last criticism)

You'll probably know this if you've played the game for a bit but something I should probably put in this review is the advice to: "Save Often". You don't know how many times you'll mess up. Maybe you entered a cave and save at the wrong time, following this, some creatures block your exit and you're too weak to fight- I recommend you save in a different slot before you enter new locations. Or it could be as simple as choosing a funny dialogue option and having the receiver of the comment initiate on you - and no... there's no "it was just a prank, bro" options. I have found the only ways out of this are to reload or kill the companion - if it's Ian carrying all your loot: you're f***ed, good luck carrying several hundred pounds of loot back to The Hub. Please take note of this, because it can add up to hours of progress being lost if the only save you can use is relatively old. Just saving your hide before you make the mistake!

Enjoy this game... and then play the sequel! 
Also thanks for taking the time to read my review!

How to start to describe one of the greatest games ever made? Well.. that's probably one of the reasons why I never did a review.

Fallout has been, still is and probably will always be my favourite game (series) of all time. Ever since I first laid eyes on the game, somewhere back in 1997, I wish I could live in that same apocalyptic world. The perfect blend of a post-nuclear environment and 50's style, makes it unique and is the reason why I would pick this game over other great games like Baldurs Gate or Planescape Torment. 

Like many RPG's, you start of creating your character. Besides sex, there are no cosmetic changes. You do get to alter your skill points and perks. Depending how you create your character, you might get a whole different adventure, each time. Play as a female? You might get some unique conversations. Low intelligence? You can't even speak properly. 

The gameplay is real-time but turn-based in combat. You can do actions, based on your Action Points (AP) and so do your enemies. You can even aim on one of your enemies' parts; cripple his leg, shoot his head or bust his groin... it's all up to you. Your opponents often die in gruesome ways and there are tons of different weapons (melee, guns, heavy weapons, unarmed, energy), different armors for you to wear, tons of items and lots of (side) quests, so you won't get bored quickly.

The writing in the game is exceptional. Most of the dialogue are interesting and often combined with a lot of (dark) humor. In my opinion, the humor is one of the best aspects of what describes Fallout, something Bethesda never got right (in Fallout 3). Only important NPC's have dialogue, which are often voiced by (former) celebrities like Dwight Schulz & Richard Dean Anderson. The narration is done by Ron Perlman, who rightfully became a Fallout Icon, over the years.

The music, produced by Mark Morgan, is also excellent. It's without a doubt, one of the best soundtracks of any game. The experimental music creates the apocalyptic atmosphere, perfectly.  

I highly recommend Fallout to every RPG lover out there. I could write a lot more about why I like Fallout but it all comes down to this: It's simply one of those games you have to play before you die.

Where to start with this game...

'It's a classic' would be a good place to start, I guess. I have no problems say that from the outset. It's only taken me 15 years to get around to play original Fallout, but I can see without a shadow of a doubt why it's so highly regarded. 

Before you play this game make sure to download the Fallout Fixt mod, which is a very comprehensive community mod which fixes a lot of the bugs, and more importantly the resolution for modern monitors. Without this patch you'll more than likely experience a horrible rainbow pixalation effect during videos and gameplay. 

Anyway...

Fallout is a turn-based RPG series which offers you various ways to tackle the game. Do you want to be a stealthy person, creeping around, pick pocketing your way to glory? Sure, why not! Do you want to be a smooth talking kinda guy who can talk his way in and out of trouble? Go on, be that guy! What about a bookworm who can use his brain to solve puzzles. Yup! And of course you can be a mix of all three, as well as a gun totting maniac! YEE-HAW!
For my playthrough I used one of the pre-set characers (Albert) who was a Lawyer in a previous life and was set up with high charisma and speech skills. This opened up different dialogue trees throughout the game, which was nice. 

Anyway, I enjoyed this game - I enjoyed it a lot. The characters are great, the voice acting (while limited) was pretty nice (though it did give away who the 'important' characters were) and the story itself was pretty deep. The game starts, as always, with you the 'Vault Dweller' leaving your vault for the first time to explore the wastelands. You're tasked with bringing back a water chip to save your vault before everyone dies of thirst! 
There's a time limit to this, which (for me) cast a sense of urgency. Normally in Fallout games (Fallout 3 and New Vegas) I'm guilty of just going 'WHEEEEE' and exploring everywhere and not really caring what I'm doing. Yet in Fallout there's no time to explore, you've got to save lives!
... if you want to. 

You see you don't NEED to save their lives, if you don't want to. In fact, you don't HAVE to do much in Fallout if you don't want to. It's not a narrow pathed experience, you can pretty much choose how you deal with the events in the game (and the end game cutscene will reflect on this at the end). A lot of games claim to be an open experience, and the actions you take reflecting on the game world, yet here's a game from 1997 which actually does that. I'm not sure it even heralds that fact that it does this. It just gets on with being a pretty damn good game. 

This brings me on to another aspect of the game - the many different branches of the game. People react to you differently depending on what you're wearing, what you're wielding, and what you're intelligence or charisma is. I find that amaizng now (in 2014), so I can only imagine how mindblowing it was back in 1997 when the game was released. The 'simple' graphics by today's standards shouldn't distract you from what is a very complex game. There's a lot going on under the hood of this game and at times perhaps too much.
My eyes were really opened up to this towards the end of the game when I was struggling with killing a certain mob. I had went about it 'head on' and was killed a number of times. Yet, after a night's sleep I came back with a different approach, a more sneaky bastards approach and it was so much easier, and strangely satisfying. I had killed the guy and he had never even seen me.
OK, sure the wastelands were plunged into another 100 years of nuclear fallout in the process, but hey... I KILLED THE GUY!

However, even with the Fallout Fixt mod, the game can be prone to crash now and again. I'm not sure if it's the game's memory file getting too big or a conflict with Steam Overlay (wouldn't be a first), but towards the end of the game (and a lot of different quest outcomes) it started to become slightly unstable. So save REGULARLY!

Which brings me on to another thing. This is an 'old school' game. It will not autosave for you, you must take control of your own save files. If you die you won't be taken back to the next/recent checkpoint... you'll have to load up from the last point you saved. 
This was the only thing I didn't like, but in the end I learned to live with it and it made me realise how pampered I had become as a gamer. I didn't have autosaves and 10 minute interval checkpoints when I was a kid and I still played games all the time back then. Yet, here I am as a grown man crying about dying and having to go back 20 minutes in the game because I had forgot to save... a lesson in life this game has given me.
Also, this game is tough. REALLY tough. Depending on how you build your character, or which character you choose. You will die a lot.
A lot.

So in closing...

If you're looking for an old school RPG experience than I'd recommend giving Fallout a try. I appreciate at time of writing they're no longer available on the Steam Store, or GOG, but hopefully they return one day, as they deserve to be played.

THIS GAME REQUIRES THE FOLLOWING:
[Functioning Brain]

Fallout 1 is NOT your average hand-holding rpg. You have to take notes, remember conversations and sometimes think outside the box in order to complete quests and get the outcome you desire. While the game is VERY OLD, it still holds up with its story, characters, overarching themes and brutality (literal and metaphorical).

BEFORE YOU PLAY here are a few tips you should know:
1. Use numbers on the keyboard when bartering, saves you a lot of time counting caps. It even goes past 999!
2. Do NOT trade with companions, use STEAL so you can move items without bartering for them. And DON'T give them burst weapons, unless you want to cosplay Swiss cheese.
3. SAVE OFTEN! I'm not gonna sugarcoat it, your ass will die or make bad decisions you'll regret. Like dying.
4. Have fun! Don't sweat it if something is a little too challenging, go somewhere else until you get more power.

The Review:
Fallout 1 is where everything started.
One vault dweller was chosen to fix a broken water dispenser and ends up saving humanity from certain doom.
Starting off as a total nobody who was picked in a lottery as "The only hope we have" - Overseer, you must find the Thingamajig Doohickey Macguffin 3000 in order to not have everyone drink their own piss.
You'll venture out, if you don't get nibbled to death by a couple rats, and find different settlements with wildly different views and opinions on how life should be. The journey is long, tedious, outright frustrating and VERY dangerous. But most importantly, you will not return the same person, as when you left.

The combat is one of the cornerstones of this game.
If you didn't spec into Perception and Agility with guns, I shall pray for you. A proper setup will save you unnecessary pain down the line, but don't be afraid to experiment with other loadouts and SPECIAL points during subsequent playthroughs. Just remember to save before you lose 2 hours of gameplay.

Dialogue can be like its own puzzle.
Not in a "I'm so fúcking confused" way, but more so "Choosing the right or wrong lines will open or close certain doors". The game is not afraid to give you funny or badass lines that initiate combat, as it adds more humor and roleplaying opportunities to your playthrough. But for the love of god, PAY ATTENTION! Someone might be obviously lying to you and send you into a deathtrap, unless you think for a moment.

Your choices matter!
A lot of the places and people in Fallout 1 have unique endings depending on how you interacted with them. You could help kickstarting a new superpower by just rescuing 1 person. Or send a town down the road of unrestrained capitalism by favoring a certain side during a dispute. Some content is a bit monotone, but that's mostly sidequests that don't do much anyway.

To conclude:
Fallout 1 has A LOT to offer if you sit down and play by its rules. You could read the wiki and get everything you want your first time, but I recommend just giving it a shot blind. After that, it's all up to you how future playthroughs go.
Overall, this is a perfect RolePlaying Game that gets a 10/10 (If the other reviews didn't make that clear already)

[h1]Fallout: A Post Nuclear Role Playing Game (like none other).[/h1] [i]Well, except for its sequels.[/i]

If you're like me and had only ever played the modern Fallout's; loved those, but are tentative about the classics for their age and intimidating design, you probably should be. That doesn't, however, excuse you from playing the original Fallout, because it's a [b]god-damn masterpiece[/b] as far as narrative and roleplaying are concerned; two things you should care about immensely as a Fallout fan. The experience of playing this game while knowing vast swathes of the lore due to Fallout: New Vegas and Fallout 3 (kinda) gave me such a close, but surreal connection to this game; it was as though the lore I knew was being brought to life in a way that shouldn't have been possible, because I'd always viewed Fallout's narrative as just that, [i]lore.[/i] It's not though. The legend of the Vault Dweller is real, and it’s tangible.

It's been almost 90 years since the Great War; when the world was plunged into nuclear chaos fighting over the last drops of energy on Earth. Your ancestors were lucky enough to escape the apocalypse however, taking shelter in Vault 13, an impenetrable underground fortress designed to house 1,000 people for dozens, possibly hundreds of years following a nuclear holocaust. Now however, in the year 2161, your vault has a problem. The water chip that regulates the vault's water supply has broken down and can't be repaired, and without a new one Vault 13 will have no more water to keep its residents alive. Thus, with a heavy heart, the vault's overseer tasks the player with venturing into the unknown wastes of California to find a replacement, giving you only 150 days until everyone you know dies of thirst.

After the introduction you get to create your character, which is when Fallout really starts. I suggest that you take your time and craft the persona you will be roleplaying as wisely, using your limited knowledge of the game world to decide what type of person you want to be, and what strengths you'd prefer to use while surviving in the ruins of California. No matter how you build your character you won't have an easy time in Fallout, but it'd be most beneficial to pick a skill or two to invest in deeply, and then rely on them as much as possible. A "well rounded" character isn't quite achievable, in other words.

In Fallout's brutal world you will find many things, but above all else you will find enthralling and captivating places. There are 13 specific locations to explore to be exact, all of which are cleverly designed, and a depressing pleasure to marvel at in terms of what the world has become. The overbearingly bleak atmosphere of each location in the game is palpable, and represents Fallout perfectly. These devastated places have secrets too, and all of them beg to be discovered...

Though I'm actively ignoring many of the more basic parts of Fallout's presentation because I see it as unimportant at this stage in the games lifespan, I'd be remised if I didn't mention the phenomenal ambient music, which is tied to the different locations. In a word, Fallout's soundtrack is [i]timeless[/i], and offers some of the most iconic melodies in gaming history.

The distinct characters and factions in Fallout, similarly to the locations, also add a great deal of world building. Each faction and character exudes the classic Fallout aesthetic, and builds another layer upon the all-important lore this game establishes. Every personality is worth lending your ear to, and many of them will give you pause, either to ponder their importance to the game, or to realize how effectively they grow on you in one way or another.

A portion of these places, factions, and people will provide you with quests of course, many of which seem mundane on the surface, but I promise you, almost none of them are. Among their individual themes, they all provide something essential to a roleplaying game; a gameplay-arc that can translate to a character-arc for the person who you have crafted. If you immerse yourself into Fallout effectively, you'll see how this gameplay-arc is formed by the quests, and how the Vault Dweller's reactions to them are malleable to your own narrative vision; making them yet another valuable tool in your roleplaying arsenal.

Ending off the nearly all-encompassing topic of the games world, I'd like to simply state that there are consequences for your actions, a majority of which can be unforeseen. These mutated wastes will shift with time whether you're aware of it, or not. Take great care in all of your choices.

Now that I've thoroughly praised the game, I should mention the few problems I do have with it. First and foremost, the turn-based combat is simply not for me. I can't help but be woefully bored during some of the larger combat sequences due to how painstakingly long it can be between the player's turns as 15 other people take theirs as well. You can set combat to play at a faster rate, but then a new problem arises as the system begins to feel unnatural in all of its sped up motions. Even in rare moments where the combat system does come together sleekly, the tedium of what you do in battle is still present, because you're never going to have a wide array of flashy fighting tactics; just the repetitive animations of shooting, stabbing, moving, and so on. I wouldn't say I hate the turn-based combat, that's too harsh a term, but after a couple hours every non-unique fight scenario just felt like a slog.

My only other qualm with the game is also brought about by Fallout's age, which is the sometimes unfair difficulty. Don't get me wrong, I love the "figure it out yourself" nature of Fallout that has essentially no hand-holding, but sometimes what the player should and shouldn't do is so poorly conveyed that you can get yourself into sticky situations. And because of the manual-save system, these scenarios can potentially ruin an entire playthrough, or at least cause you to loose hours of progress. Add in the fairly buggy disposition of Fallout and the fact that saves made in combat have a tendency to corrupt, and some frustrating moments are born. I was able to go through the game with minimal aggravation, but you may not be so lucky. Save often, and use all of your save slots.

Now, a final reminder on the best part of Fallout: the roleplaying. I've talked about it already, but I'd like to emphasize once again just how much narrative and creative freedom is handed to the player to craft their own character and personality. Ample amounts of choices are written for you to express this personality throughout the game, so take advantage of them. If deep and complex roleplaying systems are something you know how to utilize, Fallout will be a dark and twisted fantasy come to life for you.

The singular experience that is Fallout took me roughly 24 hours to complete, and while I didn't enjoy every minute of it, every [i]second[/i] certainly added purpose and value to my time in post-nuclear California. If you consider yourself a Fallout fan, you owe it to yourself to play through this game in order to get a real sense of where Fallout truly began; because simple research on the original Fallout doesn’t do it enough justice.

Few series’ have ever surpassed Fallout in excellence in my eyes (I can realistically only name one), but not a single game I can think of transcends Fallout: A Post Nuclear Role Playing Game, in setting up such a vast and remarkable franchise. This, is a game for the eons, and one which strode into the annals of gaming history like it owned the place.

This is it. The Post-Apocalyptic RPG game that began a revolution and changed everything about the genre.

PROS:

- Well written story that will keep you interested until the end.
- Charismatic and very well developed characters.
- Karma and choice system (every positive and negative choice you made will count for the rest of the adventure).
- Complex and complete interactive system and turn-based combat system.
- The precise aiming system allows you to play strategically in battles (disable an enemy specific limb, blind it, stunt it, etc).
- The S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system gives the game an amazing way to improve the main protagonist skills/perks.
- High quality 2D graphics with exceptional animations (for its time) that gives the characters/enemies great personality and a unique style.
- Music that gets you into a decadent atmosfere on a wasted and post-apocalyptic Earth.
- Excellent voice acting (many of those actors are highly recognized stars from the cinema and TV)
- Innovative buying/selling and trading system.
- Very accurate Point-and-click controls for pointing enemies, weapons, items, lockers, treasure chest, etc.

CONS:

- A pair of minor graphical glitches due to its age.

If you love turn-based RPGs, you like the atmosphere from the Mad Max movies and you don't care to travel in time to the 90's (technologically speaking). this game will assure you hours of fun and satisfaction.

[b]My Score: 9/10[/b]

Note: Played it on Windows XP - SP3

Young generation today has everything oldschools didn’t have: fast internet, cheap flight tickets, wireless gadgets and safe sex. Living now is amazing, it’s a brand new world. But there is something, that they will never have – a chance to experience original Fallout firsthand, back when it was a revolutionary game, unbiased by diverse modern market. That thing alone is worth everything.

I was s.p.e.c.i.a.l. enough to live at the time where Fallout brought life to RPG’s and set the standards for reactive worlds. It is a medium where choice and consequence exists on a game level, not on a pamphlet that comes with it. Its strong features haven’t yet been surpassed by any other game. Not only Fallout has a very distinctive gritty and honest writing style, but the dialogues actually go beyond [i]“tell me about [insert subject]”[/i] lazy excuse of a chit chat simulation you’d usually expect. It’s not “functional” content; it has a soul, man.

It is said that Fallout 1/2 fans are as dedicated as American football cheerleaders. That’s an understatement. Rumor goes that when Fallout: BOS came out a major disappointment, Interplay’s forums were flooded with so much spam that it crashed the servers.

World of original Fallout was so diverse, that developers created the Fallout Bible – a collection of texts that answer many game related questions. If you’re thinking Warhammer Codex, you’re on the right path. All this by a small development studio Black Isle and a budget that would fund Blizzard’s coffee break. Pretty damn impressive.

So what is it that makes Fallout the holy grail of video role-playing games? To understand what made it such a unique experience for the dirty, gum chewing, VHS watching, Lewis wearing rat slayers of the 90s, imagine it as the Doom of all RPG’s. It was like a Pokemon explosion – nobody knew such thing can exist, and one day it’s there. When my character got it’s way to the world map for the first time, and I suddenly realized I’m free, completely free to go anywhere, talk to anyone and do anything, that blew my godd*mn circuits out. At that time in games you had corridors and triggers. That’s it. And suddenly you get a game that has the most compelling world simulation to date. No, they won’t ask you to feed your character, make him sleep or dress him like a Barbie girl. Instead Fallout offers NPC’s that one can relate to, compelling quests, believable life stories, freedom to play however you like whoever you like. It’s a game where shooting that villain is especially satisfying because it’s not required. In fact, you yourself can be the villain.

Fallout offers a world of yellow teethed raiders that r*pe women. Homeless kids that steal cash. Drunken junkies, slu*s and drug addicts. There is r*cism, strong language and killable children. It’s a world of pain and suffering which will make you appreciate the good guys. It will tease, insult, deceive you, throw in some suspicious friends and tempt you to join your enemies. And in the end of the day, it will make a cynical remark, pretending not to be serious at all.

The original Fallout is a turn based RPG.  You create, control, and level up a single character, but you can also recruit others to your cause.  Unfortunately, followers can only have their weapons upgraded in the vanilla version of the game; however, with Fallout Fixit, they can level up and have the armor upgraded like in Fallout 2.
     The game is short by RPG standards -only about 20 hours- but a low price should offset such concerns.  Furthermore, the time that you do spend in game is what I refer to as quality game play time;  in other words, there are no boring and repetive quests or other filler content that increases game time without really adding to the game.  Your time spent in Fallout 1 will be filled with lighting raiders on fire, taking headshots on super mutants, performing unique side quests, and collecting all manner of new and destructive weapons.
     Unfortunately, Fallout 1 is not without it's flaws.  For one, the grapics are quite dated.  If beautiful graphics are a requirement for you, then you might want to skip this one.  Second, the inventory interface is rather clunky.  Such an interface would probably be considered unacceptable by modern standards, but it's not bad enough that it should destroy your ability to enjoy the game.  Finally, there are other small concerns (such as the inability to move followers that get in your way).  However, these are mostly fixed by the Fallout Fixit patch.  In fact, I highly recommend this patch (see the Steam Forums or do a Google search).  It restores some cut content, makes followers more useful/powerfull, includes the high resolution patch, and much more.
     The game may be showing its age when it comes to graphics and a clunky interface, but RPG lovers willing to look past these flaws will find a diamond in the rough.  The RPG mechanics are quite satisfying and the world and atmosphere are so captivating, that even after 15 years and 4 other Fallout games, fans still can't get enough.

Typically, when you go back into your childhood bin of toys, you find simple blocks, puzzles with four large pieces, a few zoo animals, and a bunch of broken crayons. They had their time; they were there to build motor skills, improve hand-eye coordination, and inspire creativity and imagination..... Fallout 1 is not one of those simple toys. When you reach back into your childhood bin of old games, and find this one, you quickly remember that it was not there to appeal to your childhood sensibilities. Games like this were ruthless. Games like this seperated those who took the challenge, got slaughtered, and kept coming back for more, from the rest who would scoff at the graphics or perhaps had short attention spans... people who wanted instant gratification. Games like this were the exact opposite of nuturing. They threw you into complex peril and left the world for you to figure out, to play as you saw fit.

Fallout is a open world tactical turn-based R.P.G. developed by Interplay Inc. and published by Bethesda Softworks. The game takes place in post-apocalyptic Southern California in the year 2161 decades following the Great War between the United States and China which brought the entire world to the brink of destruction at the hands of nulcear fire. The protagonist, referred to as the Vault Dweller, is tasked with recovering a water chip in what's left of civilization above ground, known as the Wasteland, to replace the broken one in their underground fallout shelter known as Vault 13. Afterwards, the Vault Dweller must then thwart the plans of a group of mutants led by a grotesque entity named the Master. This title will take you on a truly fantastic adventure through a dangerously irradiated land of men and monsters as you attempt to save your friends and family in the Vault before time runs out...GET THAT DAMN WATER CHIP!!! This title is the very first entry in the epic franchise that has enthralled and entertained many many gamers for decades and it is also a wonderful starting point to new gamers interested in the Fallout Universe.

The combat in Fallout is turn-based and is simply amazing...there is just no other way to say it. When a battle initiates, the action pauses giving you or your opponent the time to execute their attacks, move position, swap weapons or use chemicals such as healing and combat stimulants. Combat ends when either you or your opponents successfully take down or run off all their adversaries. The fighting in this game is very tactical and you will need to be smart and strategic in order to be victorious or you WILL die horribly time and time again. And don't forget about V.A.T.S., The Vault-Tec Assisted Targeting System, which allows the player to target specific body parts during combat. Buyer beware because the death sequences in Fallout are extremely violent and bloody from the decapitations to the eviscerations by mini-gun. Gory or not, the terrific gameplay is what makes the turn-based combat in Fallout so spectacular. So the next time you run across a group of raiders and one of them says "I hope you have cool stuff?!"...be ready for a fight or a very fast flight!

Visually, the game is played in a top down isometric format so fans of old school R.P.G.'s like me will feel right at home with this title but those accustomed to 3D games may find it a little off putting. Nevertheless, Fallout is good old fashioned R.P.G. gold that no fan of this genre should pass up. I have always liked isometric games as they just seem to have a beauty about them that few other genres can match. With that said, even though the events of the title take place in the burned out remnants of a once great country, the locations that you visit, as destroyed as they are, seem varied and unique. From the steel plated sterile safety of the Vault, through the horribly irradiated deserts of So-Cal, to the pieced together shanty towns of the post apocalyptic era and beyond be prepared for a journey that will take you to many interesting if dangerous places.

Fallout is a truly phenomenal title that kicked off the start of a much loved franchise and after playing this game one can definitely understand why. There is so much here that simply could not be contained in just one game such as the lore, the combat, the sense of exploration and decisions that matter and actually affect the story. These are the things that the super fans as well as the regular fans crave and also why we continue to flock to this series in all it's incarnations as the years roll by. My first exposure to the Fallout universe was Fallout 3 then New Vegas, Fallout 1, Fallout 2 and finally Fallout 4. And given the difference in gameplay between the earlier titles versus the later games I thought there would have been a disconnect but shockingly there was not. I got the same sense of immersion and satisfaction playing Fallout 1/2 that I did with the newer 3D versions of the game which really surprised me. Sadly, given the age of the title the available options are a little lax but there are Steam Achievements and Steam Trading cards to collec...PSYCH!!! This game...she a little old 'doe so you ain't gonna get none of that. But Acheivements and Trading cards are not what makes a game great it's the gameplay and this is where the title shines. Also, given the vast amount of ways to build your character plus the different decisions to make, the replayability of this game is extremely high. Without a doubt, this title is a R.P.G. in the truest sense of the word. Fallout is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED to open world, action/adventure and turn-based R.P.G. gamers.

Believe it or not I made it all the way to 2016 without playing a Fallout game but boy am I glad I decided to start at the beginning. 

Nearly 20 years after its initial release and this game still holds up. Like a fine wine or some scrumptious cheese it has indeed aged quite nicely. Although, I understand that this game may not be to everyones taste - much like that of the aformentioned wine and cheese. The dated graphics (and no, mods can't fix that) as well as the turn based combat may be an instant turn off for some people but I urge you not to judge this game at face value. This game is genuinly engrossing if you just take the time to sit down and immerse yourself in this masterfully crafted world. Your time will not be wasted. 

You can be what you want right from the start of the game you have the option of creating a completely customised character, which I strongly recommend. Even before the game has begun the entirely open ended adventure is presented to you. You have full command over the person YOU want to be. Do you want to be an honest man of the people? Skilled with a number of weapons, but only willing to draw on those who deserve it. A vicious psychopath? One who detests guns and craves blood with his bare hands. A free peace loving care free individual? Whom always uses their medicinal substances with the utmost responsibility of course. You can even play as a mentally damaged individual, struggling through day to day life and conversation in the wasteland if you so choose. Your adventure is unique.

Another thing, the writing in this game is superb, and at times, downright hilarious. Just be prepared to do a lot of reading. In essence this game is a text based adventure with an isometric skin on the top. Which brings me to the animations, which are oozing with detail. Holstering weapons, enemy attacks and death animations in particular which always seem bring a smile to my face - although probably for the wrong reasons. 
Not to fear, it isn't just silent reading with some fancy moving pictures thrown in to keep you entertained. The audio is a real treat. Each settlement you encounter throughout your journey across the wasteland plays host to a unique soundtrack that does wonders for world building. On top of this, some key NPCs have completely voiced dialouge. In a game of this age a cringe fest of audio is to be expected yet you are pleastly surprised when you are treated to an atmospheric soundtrack and wide variety of  excellent voice acting. Seriously, wandering into a new settlement for the first time and being blown away by the diversity in the voiced dialouge is quite entertaining. I could go on about the writing of the questlines and dialouge or numerous amusing allusions to various pop culture icons...

But I won't. 
Becuase this truely open ended experience is just that. An experience. To go on any longer threatens to ruin the magic of the unknown and adventure that is [b]Fallout[/b].

Released in late 1997, Fallout is the classic turn-based, post-apocalyptic RPG that kick-started an entire beloved franchise. In 1994, developer (and at-the-time publisher) Interplay Entertainment acquired the license to the GURPS RPG system and set out to create a spiritual successor to the the successful 1988 RPG of a similar theme, Wasteland. Known under the original title as Vault 13, Fallout's gameplay takes a strong influence from the early XCOM installments, namely UFO Defense. It wasn't until much later that Bethesda Softworks acquired the rights to the famed franchise.

You are a dweller from Vault 13, and the Overseer has laid upon you an important task that could mean life or death for your family and friends. The water-chip that's responsible for purifying and distributing the irradiated water from the surface and into the vault has malfunctioned, and you need to find a new one. The vault only has 150 days worth of water left, and while this may sound like a large amount of time, you will come to find that traversing the wasteland is far more time consuming and dangerous than anyone could've expected. Though this is your primary goal, it isn't your only and final one, as you will come to find out. Many people will require your help, and for better or worse it's in your best interest to help, or betray, those in need.

It's impossible to accurately remark on just how well crafted the story of Fallout is, but you can guarantee that it will be one of the best and most immersive gaming experiences of your life. That is, so long as you take the time to fully explore each of the 12 locations, and talk with nearly every named NPC that you come across; there are dozens of them, by the way. Most will have an enthralling tale or two to dish out, and many will burden you with new quests. Much of the game does require a lot of reading, although all of the main characters that you will interact with have voice-overs and a talking 3D render of said person's head. A lot of the NPC models are recycled, including those of your companions, a feature that can quickly become annoying in combat, but special NPCs always look different; some, such as the ghouls, are especially grotesque and surprisingly detailed for the era of the game.

That said, given its retro graphics Fallout has a well-developed, deep and brooding atmosphere. This is largely provided by the unforgettable ambient soundtrack, that's one of the best video game scores that will ever grace your ears. Some areas sound more sci-fi and alien, while others are horrific and droning. There are some upbeat tracks, mostly found in town locations, but these are few and far between. The environments are richly detailed, especially later on into the game when you end up stumbling upon quite a bit of gore and toxic waste moats. The poverty of the wasteland is felt with its decrepit buildings, and entire towns built out of scrap metal and junk.

Though everything about it has aged remarkably well, unfortunately not everything in this classic adventure is all nukes and rainbows, there are a few minor pain-points that become increasingly irritating over the course of the 10-20 hours you will end up investing in a playthrough. First and foremost, your companions, AKA your pack-mules. They will absolutely door-block you every single chance that they get. You see, one does not simply pass through an NPC, meaning that as your companions follow you, then can wedge you into a spot. This leaves you with no other choice than to reload your last manual save. Though it's rare to get stuck to that degree, it does happen, but you will constantly get blocked from accessing a door. Fallout also suffers from minor pixel-hunting syndrome. You want to use that rope/door/ladder/locker/body, or lockpick it, or use science, or repair it, or disarm a trap? You will be clicking a few times over for the smaller objects.

Nearly all of the main franchise staples all started here; chances are, if you're reading this review you've either played or have seen someone play Fallout 3 or 4, or New Vegas. Radscorpions, Super Mutants, Nightkin, Deathclaws, Stimpacks, Rad-X, Psycho, Power Armor, The Brotherhood of Steel, Gun Runners, Crimson Caravan, Bottlecaps, Nuka-Cola, Great Khans... the list could just keep going on and on. If you've played New Vegas prior to this title, then you will more than notice that many of the factions and stories are related back to this classic to some degree; even the New California Republic are recognized here briefly, as the location of the game takes place in California, more specifically Los Angeles and its surrounding areas. There are also some worthwhile Easter Eggs to keep an eye out for, at least for fans of the newer games,

Character customization and leveling is nearly the same here as it is in all of Fallout's predecessors; there's the S.P.E.C.I.A.L system, accompanied by perks and skills. The good/evil karma system is also in place. You level up with experience points, though level gains are very slow and the cap is 21. It's highly unlikely that you will reach the level cap upon completion of the game, unless you get every bonus and kill every NPC and enemy. The combat system is turn-based, and you have a certain amount of action points, AP, to use per turn. AP is used to do anything from moving, to shooting, reloading, changing weapon slots, etc, therefore a certain amount of strategy is involved. However, if you've decked your character out the latter portion of the title becomes child's play.

Speaking of children, this IS the edited/censored version of Fallout. There are no children in this game. For those unaware, Fallout suffered a lot of controversy and criticism since it allowed players to kill children, and even encouraged doing so at certain points. It is said that there are some working mods to introduce the censored content back in, but doing that is up to your own discretion. There's already a fair amount of gore strewn about the wasteland, and I personally suggest taking the Bloody Mess perk from the beginning to get more gruesomeness out of each kill; if you're into that type of thing, anyway. 

For a game that is two decades old, it's amazing that Fallout can still rival modern releases to a certain extent. It has an unforgettable story, with environments, characters, and soundscapes that are equally as captivating. It also helps that there are multiple endings that unfold, depending all on how you've chosen to play the game. There are also a multitude of ways to go about reaching the end, so the replayability factor here is huge. If you loved Fallout: New Vegas in particular, it's worth your while to visit this original classic in order to deeply appreciate all of the odes to it that were included. Oh Fallout, where do I begin? You aren't like many games I have played before, that's for sure.

For those of you who don't know, the Fallout Franchise is a series of games that try to help the player imagine themselves in a scenario where they are stranded in a Post-Apocolyptic Wasteland and must tackle on the many foes and challenges (including a main story and some side quests) that can be found, while inhabiting the ruins of the America. 

Despite these cool and interesting ideas I have just laid down for you, the game was almost totally different. I can't remember the full details, but something about a monkey, space, time travel and a whole slew of crazy and whacky ideas that came out of Tim Cain's head. 

If you don't know who the hell Tim Cain is, he is the guy who came up with these exact ideas and tried to make them a reality. He was also the creator and main developer for the game when it was in its humble beginnings. According to an interview, he wasn't able to work on the game in his work time (since the company refused to allow him to use its resources for his own project, sort of proving the company originally had no confidence in the project) and so he would spend his free time asking other people if they would like to test the game and provide feedback (with the promise of pizza being provided for them, if they did). Some people were so fascinated by what they saw when play testing the game, that they even offered to help on the game for free, out of pure passion for the project. Once Interplay Entertainment realised how much of a big deal the game was becoming, it reconsidered Fallout as a potential IP.

However, the original developers (Interplay Entertainment) lost the rights to the franchise's IP and it was eventually continued by Bethesda Softworks and although I do like the Bethesda games, especially for how easy and fun they are to mod. I much prefer these older Fallout Games, because they really bring out the creativity of writing and the storylines are far better than any Bethesda game, I have ever played.

There are so many Complex choices, with varying degrees of concequence. Do I help the good guy and let this town prosper? Or do I help the bad guy and watch the same town become a cesspool of raiders and bandits? Some of the choices in this game where so daring and "out there" at the time, that they straight-up removed them for fear of detracting the players experience.

Even killing children is possible in this game, however, they were completely removed from the European version of the game, because my whole entire home contitent is a bunch of plebs who can't understand the nuance behind a piece of fictional media.

There are also many unique characters, that you are bound to stumble upon, when exploring the Wastes. Most of which are bundled-in with some great voice acting (for the late 90s) and some hand-sculpted/painted face models that help bring these characters alive.

What really caught my attention, in regards to the whole entire Fallout series, was that it has a very interesting setting/time period. Especially when you consider how it is a branch of our very own timeline. 

It is believed that the Fallout Universe is completely diverged from the real-world timeline, sometime after World War II. Imagine then, a world where the capicator isn't even invented and instead, most first world countries end up focusing entirely on Atomic/Nuclear Solutions for both energy and warfare. Since most of the resources were beggining to dry up, this caused many of the nations to wage war and fight for control over them. This became known as the 'Resource Wars'.

Eventually, China ended up declaring war on USA. Invading Alaska for their oil and putting America in a tough position. This kicked off the Sino-American War that raged on for around 11 years, before resulting in a nuclear exchange between both China and America. 

This is where Fallout's Post-Nuclear, Apocolyptic feel and environments spring from.
For you see, when playing the game, you won't just stumble upon rats, moles, scorpions or dogs. They are irradiated and can withstand more than a simple shot to the face. With this radiation (which is from the nuclear warheads brought on by China), comes other threats, like Ghouls, Super Mutants and Deathclaws. Deadly creatures that will usually attack on sight.

With all these threats, comes the neccessity to always be prepared and to always save your game around every corner. Trust me, if you're new to this game then you will either do one of two things:

A) Die a horrible death to some OP monster that you weren't prepared for.
OR
B) You run out of time for your first quest. Resulting in the death of your Vault.

Now, you might be saying to yourself "okay, I understand the nasty creatures, but what do you mean by running out of time for the first quest?" Well, you see, Fallout's first quest is a timed quest. It's not anything like "do this in 5 minutes or else you fail" but it's more along the lines of "If you don't get this essential piece of equipment to fix our water supply, then everyone is going to die of dehydration" and I will be honest, I am usually against these kinds of quests. Especially in a Role-playing Game, where anything can be done at literally any point that you want it to. However, it makes a lot of sense here. After all, the whole point of the game is to feel alone and isolated - but at the same time, in a constant rush and fear of what will happen if you don't act upon something quick. Like finding the things you need to survive. If you ask me, that sounds a lot like living a desolate wasteland.

There is only one issue that I have with the early Fallout games (although, I have honestly grown into it in the past few years) is that their combat was turn-based. This might of been bareable in 1997, but since I hadn't played these games before, it really bugged me at first and caused me to just play the game in increments at a time. However, as soon as I started to understand the strategy behind the turn-based combat, I felt myself enjoying the game more and levelling up became a breeze.

I highly recommend anyone to play this, if they are into oldschool RPGs (with an interesting twist, because it isn't fantasy), laced with dark humor and the ability to literally shoot anyone in the face. AND GROIN!

Fallout is a isometric, free roam, turn based (combat only), role playing game. I found to be a great game, although yes it is dated and hasn't aged well in graphical terms. The content and story I found great and enjoyed every minute.

Considering its release date of [b]1997[/b], it still is overall a brilliant game, anyway let me explain myself.

[h1]The Game Play[/h1]
Before you start on your journey you are able to create a character. With various options and choices related to a point based skill system, that is also commonly used in the later fallout games.

After character creation you are put in the shoes of a dweller of vault 13, sent out into the desolate wastelands save the vault.

[h1]Difficulty[/h1]
The difficulty of the game is, let's say unforgiving if you are unprepared. I must admit I died quite a few times walking into places I didn't belong or starting fights with bigger stronger characters.

Hopefully you will find your demises just as funny as I found mine. (Save regularly)
In the options you can set the difficulty of the games combat system in your favour. I left this at a default state to enjoy the game as it was intended.

[h1]Controls & Interface[/h1]
I cannot say I am a fan of the control system but for the age of the game I can see why the controls were done in this way. Although once you get the hang of them it become straight forward.

First of all they are a little hard to get use to as there is no definitive tutorial and is based on a left click and right click system with a hold function, the keyboard is not necessarily required.

The inventory system is simple and works well, although for future games I hope to see much more functionality. It uses a drag and drop system with hold click as well.

[h1]Achievements[/h1]
This game has no steam achievements. Which I think increased my enjoyment of the game.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The plot of the story I found to be great as it gets you stuck in straight away. By giving you a lengthy time limited quest to save the people of your vault right away gives you a sense of urgency. I found the main quests and side quests fun which kept me coming back for more. 

The ending I found was very fitting and I hope anyone who plays through the game enjoys it as much as me.

[h1]Combat System [/h1]
The combat is turn based, with each turn you have action points (AP) relating to how much agility you have including traits that can give you extra AP's for a turn. What you do in combat is up to you although everything will have a cost of AP you could if you fancy shoot your own allies or miss the enemy and accidently vaporise your ally.

[h1]Skills & Traits[/h1]
Every time you level up you get to put points into certain skills and every three levels you can choose a trait, not counting the two you can choose on character creation.

I chose traits and skills on how I wanted to build my character some of them you will find useful and some you won't. Try saving before hand to test ones out. So you're not stuck with something you don't find useful.

[h1]Sounds  & Effects[/h1]
Due to the age of the game the sounds are still pretty decent and fitting for the wasteland environment.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The graphics although dated for game that came out in 1997 are still pretty good, although trying to find items on the floor can be a little challenging.

[h1]Cut Scenes[/h1]
The cut scenes, death scenes and endings are great, although dated now I still enjoyed them.

[h1]Humour & Trivia[/h1]
I liked the games humour and spent a good few hours on the fandom wiki. I liked that Dogmeat is a reference to [i]Madmax 2[/i] which was completely unexpected.

[b]Woof![/b]

[h1]Game Utilities[/h1]
Be careful the game does not offer a auto save function so any vault dweller must be extra careful before taking important actions. Whether it is stealing from or killing an innocent civilian or starting a fight with a super mutant.
You may end up quite dead.

[h1]Multiplayer[/h1]
This game is single player only and does not contain any multiplayer. Although you can hire non player characters (NPC's) as mercenaries to follow you around on missions. Which is highly useful so long as you don't accidentally shoot them instead of your enemies. 

[h1]Bugs - [i]Important[/i][/h1]
Unfortunately fallout has a tendency to crash at random times which I presume is based on the fact it was not meant to run on newer versions of windows.

[b]So vault dwellers I recommend you save regularly.[/b]

[i]Also be wary of tabbing out, many have reported not being able to get back into the game although the game seems minimised. 

This not necessarily true hover down in the left hand corner above the task bar and you will find an invisible box click it and should maximise fallout.[/i]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Overall I found this game very fun to play, par the minor crashes and issues with tabbing out. This game may be dated by modern game standards.

I personally think this is a fantastic game and hopefully never forgotten, if you ever have the chance to play and you have played any of the fallout games I strongly recommend you play this one.

Even twenty years after release, Fallout 1 has proven itself to be not just a pinnacle of post-apocalyptic science fiction, but RPGs as a whole. 

I played Fallout 1 after 3 and New Vegas (3 is okay but NV is in my top 5 games of all time), and at first I hated it- it was a far cry from Bethesda's first-person Fallouts, and it was pretty overwhelming to leave Vault 13 into a wasteland that did not hold my hand. This was back in 2013 (or 2014, I don't really remember), and I picked the game up again after a "hiatus" for lack of a better word. It was around this time that I have experienced the immaculate dumpster fire that is Fallout 4, and replaying Fallout 1 with this in mind- holy shit I fucking loved it.

The immersive atmosphere is what will always make this game stand out- it's downright oppresive at points [spoiler] especially in areas such as Necropolis, the Military Base, the Glow, and the LA Boneyard. [/spoiler]  This atmosphere is paired well with the lack of hand-holding in the game, as you are let out into the wasteland to do whatever your heart desires: save a village, root out political corruption, shoot innocents in the streets (you know, the usual). The only thing that the game directly tells you, in regards to the game world, is what your primary goal is in the game, to save your Vault.

Seguing into the story, it's a simple story told expertly well with interesting characters and an equally interesting world being built around you. Characters such as [spoiler] Harold, the Master, Overseer Jacoren, Tandi, and Set [/spoiler] will always be memorable to me because of the sheer amount of intrigue that ooze from them; now think of any memorable characters in Fallout 4... you probably have one particular in mind, not because he is interesting, but because he is bland and annoying.

I keep ridiculing Fallout 4 in this review, but I can't compare its combat system to that of Fallout 1's because they are incredibly different from one another. Fallout 1 has turn-based combat, so it  comprises of a cycle of turns that the player, companions, neutrals, and enemies, and it requires a degree of patience in order to deal with; in fact, the combat is one of the reasons me in 2013/14 gave up on it so early. To fight your foes, you have the V.A.T.S. system, which allows for targeting specific body parts: aim at the eyes for a chance at an instant-kill, aim at the arms to disarm your foes, shoot at the legs to slow them down, so on so forth. Combat is also very challenging- you will likely die a lot during your first playthrough, and these deaths especially peak towards the last quarter of the game. This challenge almost makes me recommend that your first playthrough should be set on the easiest difficulty for max enjoyment, but if you like your extreme challenge, go for it. Oh, and the death animations are 10/10, you just have to see for yourself.

To conclude this already long review, I recommend Fallout 1 to those with patience for the slow gameplay and the lack of traditional tutorials, as well as to those who are interested in the Fallout franchise and gaming history as well.

There is nothing to say about Fallout 1 that hasn't been said. And yet here I go saying it again, because you can never heap enough praise on a game as good as this.

Fallout 1 is the best Fallout game. Later games in the series may have had better graphics, a broader scope or a larger focus on faction mechanics, but Fallout 1 has atmosphere. It's a darker game than its sequels (not grimdark, just dark) and succeeds at creating a wasteland that feels rough and devoid of hope while still carrying a bit (but not too much) of the series' signature sense of humour and levity. In some ways it has more in common presentationally with the Metro or Stalker series than other Fallout games. It also has a clarity of vision which hasn't been seen in any Fallout game since. It's a relatively short and narratively focused experience for an open world game, but within that focused narrative we get something a lot more thematically interesting and coherent than the often disparate and self-contained side quest stories of later entries, which often felt more like a funhouses than connected, living worlds (I'm looking at you, Fallout 2 and 3).

Lastly, Fallout 1 has the best villain in the entire series. In case you're actually new to this game and not just an old head re-purchasing it on Steam, I won't spoil anything about this character. The meeting with him/her/it should be experienced blind.

What I primarely like about Fallout 1 is how much your character build matters. Many modern RPG's have forgotten the art of emergent gameplay, of having game events defer back to the player's stats and playstyle rather than just his dialogue choices. Your experience with this game will be vastly different if you have, say, a high doctor and speech skill coupled with an intelligence of 9 than if you're playing as a combat specialist with an intelligence of 2. Whole entire swaths of conversations will change, the way you approach problem solving will change, avenues that are open for one type of character might be completely closed for others or force unorthodox solutions (like using plastic explosives to blow open a door that you can't lockpick, or using the pickpocket skill to plant grenades in enemies' inventories), and so on. It lets you forge your own path through the game in a way that picking between outcome 1, 2 or 3 in, say, a Mass Effect game simply doesn't allow for. In many ways Fallout has more in common with System Shock or Deus Ex than the modern RPG genre it helped define, because it's mechanically driven just as much as narratively.

One way to illustrate how gameplay mechanics and character build can vastly change one's experience with this game is through the mechanic of crippled limbs. If you get shot in the leg, there is a chance it will simply give out, forcing you to either heal it or find a doctor who can. As long as your leg remains crippled, you can't run. At all. This sort of scenario creates its own mini-story within the game. You're now forced to potentially spend days or weeks looking for a doctor's bag, a relatively rare item, or a doctor who can heal you, a somewhat expensive ordeal, changing your entire path through the wasteland, making you postpone otherwise important, sometimes time sensitive tasks. Unless, of course, you're a skilled doctor yourself, in which case you can fix your leg and move on. In Fallout 3 you heal a crippled limb by the press of a button, so there is absolutely no weight to it. Some might prefer that, but in my opinion Fallout 1's more unforgiving game mechanics lend weight to the notion that we are in a wasteland, and not a theme park. And it gives you a wonderful sense of player agency and success when you come across a problem that your character is uniquely equipped to solve.

Fallout 1 is a very open game in the truest sense of the word. You can technically make a beeline for the final boss the moment it begins, and there is a constant sense that the game is willing to accomodate everything you (try to) do, including stupid decisions like running headfirst into a pack of deathclaws at level 2, with very little in the way of artifical barriers, handholding or forced story moments that you can't avoid. Fallout 1 doesn't make you complete a tutorial area, it doesn't tell you which places are safe or which NPC's are trustworthy and you can completely miss certain story-important people or plot developments if you're not observant. A lot of its real storytelling takes place in the background, between the lines. There is ambiguity about the different factions and their motivations. Even its inhuman villain can be understood and sympathized with, and his entire backstory has to be pieced together rather than told directly.

Presentationally and graphically, this is obviously a very old game. It's a turn based, isometric game, which for a very long time was considered outdated and passé in the industry (though thankfully no longer). Its UI is clunky and could definitely stand to be overhauled in a major way. I'm not going to say you'll have fun immediately if you aren't used to this style of game. But with persistence Fallout 1 becomes an amazing experience, one that makes you forget its age like all timeless things do.

And when it comes to certain things like voice acting it is actually much better than later entries in the series, especially New Vegas and 3 (although, to be fair, only few characters have voices). Music and sound design are on another level too. The ambient tracks that play as you explore the wasteland sound like how a wasteland should sound. There is a reason New Vegas re-used these tracks. They definitely have a ton more character than Bethesda's forgettable background pling-plong-pling compositions that seems directly lifted from Oblivion and Skyrim.

All in all, this game is the real deal. It's the one they will dig out of the burning rubble in a hundred years when nuclear war has destroyed everything. They will then conclude that human beings, while stupid, at least understood the art of designing good RPGs.

[h2]Every meme you know was born here[/h2]
 
Boot it up and the cultural fingerprints just keep arriving. Ron Perlman opens his mouth, says "War. War never changes," and you realize you've been hearing that exact line in every trailer since the Clinton administration. The SPECIAL system is here. Vault Boy is here, giving you a thumbs up while your character bleeds out. The Pip-Boy is on your wrist. Dogmeat is in Junktown wanting to eat strangers. The Brotherhood of Steel exists and is hilariously bureaucratic about it. Power Armor, bottle caps, Nuka-Cola, Super Mutants, the Master, FEV, Stimpaks, the Vaults --> all of it. The entire post-apocalyptic aesthetic Bethesda turned into a multi-billion-dollar franchise is sitting right here, in a 1997 game that fits on a postage stamp. The fact this came from a team that briefly licensed GURPS, lost the license in March 1997 because Steve Jackson decided there was too much gore, and then casually invented SPECIAL from scratch with months left on the clock --> that should not be possible. They did it anyway.
 
[h2]It is allowed to be mean to you[/h2]
 
Modern RPGs feel like an HR-approved customer journey. Fallout 1 is the opposite. You can build a character so stupid (Intelligence 1) that NPCs refuse to dialogue with you and your character just grunts at everyone for the entire game. Skill checks fail. Quests time out and disappear forever. Children walk around the wasteland --> in the 1.0 US release you could shoot them, get the "Childkiller" reputation, and watch caravan guards execute you on sight in every other town. Europe demanded children be removed entirely, which is how version 1.2 was born. The wasteland did not care about your feelings or your build.
 
[h2]The 150-day timer, the franchise's first villain[/h2]
 
The water chip quest has a hard 150-day clock. Run out and you get a "GAME OVER" screen with the kind of casual cruelty modern games would A/B test out of existence. Underneath that ran a second 500-day super-mutant invasion timer (patched out in 1.2) and a residual 13-year hard cap because the engine literally could not represent your character existing past that. Imagine pitching that in a Bethesda meeting today --> they'd defenestrate you and then ship a 12-hour tutorial.
 
[h2]Combat is turn-based, brain-on, and slightly stupid[/h2]
 
Combat runs on action points. You aim at body parts. You can shoot somebody in the eye, miss, and watch your bullet sail across the map and kill a passing brahmin. The death animations are graphic in a goofy, low-resolution way --> people fall apart like wet paper towels and the screen sometimes gets weirdly festive about it. It's slow, it's clunky, and it's also one of the most legibly strategic combat systems any RPG has ever shipped. You can finish entire fights without the lights coming on, just by clicking carefully and reading the log.
 
[h2]Where it actually creaks[/h2]
 
Pathfinding is a war crime --> Dogmeat will walk into a forcefield, die, and there is no negotiation. The UI was designed by someone who hated mice. There's no quest log worth using, so a notebook is mandatory, and yes, a real one made of paper. Several skills (Gambling, Outdoorsman, Throwing) are functionally cosmetic. The unpatched 1.0 version has bugs that can permanently brick the main quest, so install the community patches before you start. The Hub alone will reduce a grown adult to tears.
 
[h2]Final Thought[/h2]
 
This is the bitter, refined, niche bar of dark chocolate that all the milk-chocolate post-apocalyptic games trace back to. Thirty people, three and a half years, one isometric engine, and an entire cultural template falls out of it. You are not playing Fallout 1 for comfort --> you're playing it to see what was in the room before the genre got polished, sanitized, and sold back to you as Fallout 76.
 
If you have ever quoted "War never changes," you owe this game ninety hours of your life.
 
[b]Estimated frustration-free value:[/b] €12.99 (Steam/GOG ask less, and it's worth more)
[b]Personal Note:[/b] Install Fallout Fixt before your first launch. Take [b]Gifted[/b] as a trait and tag [b]Small Guns[/b], [b]Speech[/b], [b]Lockpick[/b]. Do NOT dump Intelligence as a joke build on a first playthrough --> the dialogue is the best part of the game, and a low-INT run only lands if you've already seen what you're missing.
 
More no-filler value estimates here: [b][url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/BuyersRegret] Buyer's Regret [/url] [/b]

I’ll admit that I never played the original Fallout games. I got introduced to Fallout when playing Fallout 3. That was my first Fallout game, and because of that game I fell in love with the lore, atmosphere, and characters.

Back in the late 90s, what I considered the golden age for cRPGs, I leaned heavily into FPS and Adventure games. I tried a few RPGs like Icewind Dale, but at the time they just couldn’t hold my attention. I knew these games were good, but I was an FPS junkie back then. I remember working at CompUSA (yeah, I am that old) and one of my co-workers was going crazy about Fallout 2. He would talk about it non-stop and almost got me convinced to play it back then. But my taste in gaming just were not there yet. 

So, after many years of wanting to play the originals but never got around to it, I finally fired up the first game just a few weeks ago. Let me tell you what, it’s old and dated, graphicly it is hard to see what things are. Controls are a bit clunky, and there is little to no information other than your character stats and basic information about the items in your inventory. But don’t let that discourage you, Fallout is a legend for a reason. Thankfully you can run the game at higher resolutions, but you may not want to go higher than 1080. I tried 1440 and it was hard to reach or make out anything. 1080 or lower is best as the graphics don’t scale well on higher resolutions and figuring out what to click and pick things up can be a nightmare at higher resolutions.

Once you find your comfortable resolution, mine was 1920x1080, you get to choose one of three pre-made characters or create a custom character. I went with custom as I like to make my own and not rely on developer made characters for RPGs. Of course, if you choose custom, you can adjust your S.P.E.C.I.A.L attribute points around. I kind of cheated a bit and looked up what stats you should focus on. I am kind of glad I did because S.P.E.C.I.A.L is handled differently in this first game. Any Fallout fan will know what S.P.E.C.I.A.L means, S = Strength, P= Perception, E= Endurance, C= Charisma, I= Intelligence, A= Agility, and L= Luck. In Fallout you can ignore Charisma all together and get away with a low stat of 2, because it doesn’t really do anything. You would think it effects speech but there is a skill for that and if you make it high enough its like you had a high Charisma all along. Also, Intelligence affects speech as well. If you have low intelligence in this game your character will basically be dumber than Super Mutants and that will show up during dialog. Intelligence determines how many skills points you get when you level, so having this attribute high can help you increase your skills faster. 

Two of the most important attributes are Luck and Agility. Agility affects your action points, and you will want as many of these as possible to maximize your actions during your turn. Luck affects your chances with the dice rolls behind the scenes, high luck means better success of rolls and vice versa. Luck also affects your chance at Critical hits on a target. So having a high Luck in this game is very beneficial. I ended up with 5 points in Strength, 2 points in Charisma, 7 points in Perception, 6 in Endurance, 9 points in Intelligence, 10 points in Agility, and 9 points in Luck. These stats allowed my character to hit hard and have plenty of skill points to increase my three tagged skills.

Speaking of skills, there a about 20 or so of them ranging from Lock picking to Small guns, Repair, Speech, Stealing and so on. My three tagged skills were Small guns, Speech, and Lock picking. I picked Small guns because I found out that a majority of weapons in Fallout are classified as small. There are very few Big Guns and Energy Weapons, and you don’t see them till the end of the game, plus ammo for these weapons are expensive and hard to come by. Speech so I can succeed at Speech challenges during dialog. And Lock picking so I can open anything I needed too. These skills helped a lot during my play through, but Repair, and Steal can be good as well since some quests almost require them. Energy weapons can be a good one to upgrade slowly during your play….because if you find the Alien Blaster, it’s the most powerful weapon in the game. If you want to use it, you’ll need some points in that skill. Unlike the later Fallout games, skills are very important in Fallout. They can help you during conversations, shooting weapons, stealing things, and so forth. So, choose wisely and don’t just throw your skills anywhere. Focus on a few that matter to your play style.

Once you create your character or choose a pre-made one, you’ll begin your journey. In Fallout you are from Vault 13, the water chip for your vault has failed and you are tasked with finding a new one or in 150 days everyone will die from lack of water. The Overseer suggests that you start your search in Vault 15. This is the only location on your map right now. Once you leave the starting cave you are free to go anywhere, though you only have 150 days to get this water chip. As you travel on the main map time goes by and the days can rack up if you just decide to go all over the place. In Fallout there is no hand holding, which means you have to explore and talk to everyone to find the answers to your quests. I know the 150-day timer kind of sucks, but once you complete that main quest part two of the game opens up and you are able to explore and discover for as long as you want till the end.

Combat in Fallout is what you would expect from a cRPG game. When you are in combat, each character on screen will take their turn. Moving, going into your inventory, or attacking take up action points. But you get free actions like swapping weapons and using items in your inventory. Different weapons have different cost of action points and depending on how many attributes points you have in Agility will determine how many action points you will have during your turn in combat. So, use them wisely. When attacking you have a choice of normal attack or aim attack. Aim attack takes up more action points but it allows you to specifically choose your enemies body parts just like VATS in the later Fallout games. Your skills will determine how well you’ll hit that body part and damage taken by your target. So, focusing on one type of weapon class is key to getting best results during combat rolls. While you wait for your turn the enemies will attack you or your companions during their attack phase. Armor can help protect you from taking damage as you will get hit. You can heal outside of combat with the Doctor or First Aid skills, but during combat you can only use a Stimpak to heal. And of course there are chems. All the drugs you will be familiar with such as psycho, buff-out, mentats, etc. Drugs do last longer in this game but be careful you can get addicted to them which has negative effects. I rarely, if ever used them, found they are worth a pretty penny when selling them, which was great for making money.

Companions in Fallout are very useful, though they are squishy and once they die, they are gone forever (unless you load a save before their death). There are only four companions you can recruit and one of them is Dog Meat. You can load up your companions with stuff and have them as a pack mule, but if they die you will lose all the stuff on them unless you can carry it yourself or load them onto others. Using your companions as a pack mule is quirky. You can easily give them stuff but to get it back the game forces you to barter with them (give them something or money value equal to the item). You can get around this by using the stealing skill, since they are companions, they don’t give a shit if you steal from them. It is an odd way to trade with your companions, but it works.

Final Verdict: 5/5 Amazing Game, Legendary RPG.
