The Fallout world is my favourite fictional world, period. The lore is deep and intelligent, and packed full of interesting characters, concepts, and secrets for the player to learn about and discover. The debut Fallout game itself is a classic RPG by an measure, and one of the best RPGs of the 90s. 

While not as accessible as the most recent games in the series, Fallout doesn't lack charm and depth, and for those with the patience to tackle a game that's part classic RPG, part adventure game, it holds a wealth of wonderful fiction to discover. 

However, As much as it was a great achievement in terms of storytelling and world-building, it is a product of its time and thus suffers from some of the problems that plagued both the aforementioned genres in the 90s: clunky UI, an isometric camera that often impedes movement and blocks items and people, combat that relies utterly on chance with little skill involved, unforgiving difficulty for beginner characters, and - worst of all IMO - illogical solutions to problems that can leave unwitting players frustrated. 

[spoiler]You didn't think to use a radio on that one particular computer? Too bad, buddy, you're stuck[/spoiler]

Fallout 2 is bigger, streamlines some of the technical issues and irons out some unintuitive features, but I think that this is the superior game when it comes to plot, tone, and narrative. The fantastic voice acting from some great performers coupled with the driving storyline really draws you in and makes you feel like there is something real at stake. The narrative and the world really are the game's strongest features. Complaints aside, I do recommend that any fan of the Fallout series commit some time to discovering this game, and delving deeper into the world of Fallout.

PROS:
-Tremendous player agency. Not only does Fallout 1 give you choices to do just about anything in the game world, it also makes you feel like success or failure is up to the player. The viability of your character build, the chances of who you kill or who ends up killing you hinges entirely on the choices you make. Something that is VERY unique, especially compared to modern games.

-Rewarding advancement. Every level gives you a sense that your character is advancing in meaningful ways. Perks feel powerful and significant, your skills matter, and endgame abilities can make you feel like a powerhouse.

-Memorable characters. The story characters have unique graphics and interesting personalities that are well voice acted.

-Humor. The game has a unique sense of dark comedy that makes the game fun to play while still preserving the bleak and serious atmosphere.

-Replayability. Even after beating the game more than once there is still motivation to go back and play, making a different type of character or making different RP choices that lead to different outcomes.

-Unique aesthetic. The setting and artstyle is unlike anything else, blending retro vibes with bleak cynicism.


CONS:
-Not much to look at. Even for a 20+ year old game, the graphics are very rudimentary. There aren't that many sprite variations so many characters, including important NPCs and story characters, look like indistinguishable clones. Since the art is low-res, you're forced to either up the resolution which makes everything look tiny or lower the resolution in which case everything looks kinda pixelated. 

-Unbalanced skills. Some abilities (small guns, energy weapons, speech, gifted) are incredibly powerful while other abilities (almost everything else) are next to useless. You might actually use skills like Science or Repair maybe once or twice in the entire game. It makes the game feel like you need a guide to tell you how to make your character due to there being so many useless choices.

-Small world. While the game makes the world feel big by making you walk long distances in the overworld, there are only a handful of locations in the game. The time you take to beat the game is on par with other RPGs (about 20-ish hours) but you spend most of your time in just a few areas comprising only a few of the same tilesets.

-Slow combat. Being turn-based is okay, but the battles can at times feel like it takes forever for people in the game to do what they're doing or walk where they're going to walk, especially when there's lots of enemies in the area.


Overall though, Fallout 1 is an amazing game that produces a really unique experience that feels fulfilling in a way you don't see to much of anymore.

Fallout 1 is a game people are only familiar with because of Fallout 3. And usually, whenever someone goes back to try the game, the most common reaction is “ew, this is gross” and then they turn it off. But for the few bold souls who are willing to sit through the game’s old quirks, they can find an experience that’s deep, awing, and fun. So long as you have a guide. Hello, I’m DavyDaveDavid, and this is my ride on the Steam Train to… Fallout: A Post Nuclear Role-Playing Game.

Set in the distant future of 2161, Earth has been ravaged by nuclear war. Except for West Virginia and Las Vegas because of course, they weren’t. Plants have died out, lakes have dried up, all the land in the world is irradiated, and cattle suddenly have two heads for some baffling reason. However, many of America’s citizens have taken shelter in underground communities known as the Vaults. Their descendants still live there today, sheltering themselves from the violent world above. However, your vault, Vault 13, has started to run out of clean drinking water, after their specialized computer chip for managing purification malfunctions. So the Overseer of your vault tasks you with the mission of finding a new chip to replace the old one, completely unaware of the horrors you’re about to encounter.

Throughout the entire game, you’re racing against the clock not only to find a new water chip, but also to stop a mutant army from destroying your home. So it’s a bit tense. The whole game is projected in an isometric view and whenever you happen to run into a hostile NPC, the game switches to turn-based combat. The entire game can be played with the mouse alone, which is really good for simplicity’s sake. However, the game is built upon layers and layers of submenus around switching items, your inventory, the pause menu, your skills, the map, your character, your pipboy (which is useless in this game), and ending your turn in combat. Which is a bit intimidating for those who are only familiar with the later games. 

But once you manage to wrap your head around this game’s mechanics, is it a good time? Yes, yes it is… If you have a guide. Part of this game is all about deciphering clues given to you by characters in conversation, which is a pretty hard thing to do if you suffer from ape-brain as I do. So for those of you who don’t really have the patience to slug through the game’s dated quirks, I’d recommend having another device handy with the Fallout Wiki ready to look up whatever confuses you. Especially, since you only have 150 days in-game to find a new water chip (which isn’t very long, btw), so you really need to hurry up.

However, even without a guide, Fallout 1 is a thrilling experience. The soundtrack is so somber it fills me with more anxiety than Resident Evil wishes it could instill in me. Interacting with the few voiced characters in the game is always a delight, because they’re so jam-packed with personality it feels like I’m speaking to an actual individual. And each major area is so unique and filled with lore, it’s practically oozing mythos. It’s frickin’ great and any fan of the newer games should give it a try (especially since it’s only $10 on Steam). Until next time, I’m DavyDaveDavid, and I’ll catch you on the flipside.

For example, if you invest in the Intelligence stat, you gain more skill points at level up, gain more dialogue option, and increase skills like science and repair. Skills determine what you're good at like being able to use energy weapons more efficiently or if you are good at speech which allows you to persuade people during dialogue. Tag skills let you boost 3 different skills by 20% and and when you use skill points on them, they go up twice as fast. You can also pick optional traits which give you a positive bonus at a penalty. An example being bruiser which increases your strength stat by 2 points but losing 2 action points in the meantime. Action points what you can do during a turn in combat like pulling up your inventory, moving, or attacking.

You play as the Vault Dweller who receives a message from his overseer telling him the water chip in his and many other people's vault/ home has broken down. The Overseer tells the Vault Dweller to find another chip before the vault runs out of water. This is your first main quest of the game. At first, I hated how I had a time limit at the beginning but the amount of time you are given is actually quite generous.

 There are 2 other main quests in the game but I'm not going to mention how they work due to them being spoilers. But I'm going to say that they are easily the weakest part of the game. You're supposed to do certain tasks and there are an insane number of ways you can complete it, but the game never explains what you need to do it in the other ways and going through it the combat way is incredibly tough especially if your sequence is low. If you don't know, sequence is a stat that determines getting turns faster in combat. If you know what you're doing, these last 2 quests are fine and not that big of a problem, but if you're going through the game for the first time, you will probably spend hours getting lost unless you look it up online. 

Another negative I have with this game are the companions. They are only good at the beginning of the game like if you are going through Vault 15 for example but besides that, they are useless and were actually detrimental when I was going through the last 2 locations of the game. Dogmeat is in my opinion the worst companion due to not being able to command him to stay back. Luckily there is a mod called Fallout Fixt and it fixes most of the issues with the game including this one. I highly recommend playing with that mod because it improves the game a lot. If you are a purist, you can play a version of the mod that doesn't add new content but just fixes the technical issues. 

Even though the last section of the game isn't very good and the companions are useless, the other locations and amount of side quests you can do FAR make up for the weak parts. You can go to new locations by talking to people and asking where they are, exploring around the map and hoping to find a new location, or just by memory if you are experienced with the game. These locations like Junktown or Boneyard have more people that can lead you to your objective but you can do side missions for these areas and will have an affect on the ending of your game.

To keep track of certain things in the game the overseer at the beginning gives you a Pip-boy 2000 that can show a map of your location, tell you the time which has an effect on your game, reading holodisks with are information tapes which can help you progress in the game, and show you what quests you have from each area in the game. But there are unmarked quests which you can receive awards from but are not marked on your Pip-boy.

This was my first CRPG and I would argue it was a great place to start (especially if you are like me and can't run Baldur's Gate III). I went into this primarily as a fan of Fallout: New Vegas and that's kind of how I'm framing this review (no major spoilers though). I had come to understand that despite being in an entirely different genre, the rich and believable world of Fallout: New Vegas, along with its willingness to present tough choices with real consequences, could be traced back to the original game in the series. I wanted more of that universe and its choices, and Fallout 1 more than delivered.

That being said, the game asks a lot of you. It requires far more patience than just about any modern game I've played, and even then the reward for this patience is less tangible than, say, defeating a boss in a soulslike. This game asks you to do a lot of reading, with the reward ultimately kind of being... more reading. However mundane that sounds, the dialogue here is among the best rewards in any game I can think of. The writing is subtler than New Vegas, the comedy a little more sparse (yet equally funny), and the tone more focused... and what a tone it is. This game is *bleak*. It hasn't yet been 100 years since the bombs fell, and it shows. Civilization is only just beginning to rebuild. Fallout 1's characters take this world very seriously, because it appears they have no other choice.

Having given all that praise, on a first playthrough, I did feel like I was waving a cane in the dark. Stats are everything, so build a character poorly and you could be SOL, especially given the time limit on the main quest (the timer is actually quite forgiving, but it definitely didn't feel that way without knowing how far along the quest I was). Dialogue choices with major consequences are often not presented that way, and combat encounters come out of absolute nowhere at times. I learned to save frequently which mostly circumvented these problems, but there was definitely a good deal of frustration, especially at first. I also had to use a guide a few times, with some clues for progression being just a little too cryptic in my opinion (oldheads may disagree).

Ultimately, all of the resistance that came along with this game only made it that much more rewarding to complete. The feeling of finally taking out a Deathclaw, or repairing a robot using context clues alone and watching it clear a path forward, or realizing that the once-unintuitive controls had become second nature, or random-encountering a crashed alien spaceship, or losing a companion and choosing to let the story go on without them. Each of these moments meant a lot, and there were countless others like them.

This is definitely not a game to come home to during a stressful week at work, but it *is* a game to fall in love with on a long weekend. I highly recommend.

First of all, I'd like to state that the current 16h play time is incorrect, as I played this game extensively several years ago when I had a physical copy of the game.

TL;DR: A must for anyone that likes the Fallout series, by far one of (if not) the best Fallout.

Now let's start by what is obviously less than ideal due to the age of the game: graphics. Mind you, I personally find the graphics to still be quite good, it's just that you'll likely play at less than comfortable resolutions if you want to be able to actually see something in the game. Also, videos and some other content just wasn't made to scale to today's resolutions so expect those to be extremely pixelated.

Other than that (and even that is just an artifact of aging) the game is ridiculously good. The initial story revolves around you being picked among your vault dwellers as the one with the highest chance of survival in the outside. As such, the fate of Vault 13 rests on your shoulders. The water chip malfunctioned and your vault only has a limited supply so throughout all of the game you see the days and the hours go by and the time remaining counting down, giving you a sense of urgency as your vault's supply depletes towards zero.

The fact that time goes by as you play and travel in the wasteland places a very serious weight on your style of play. If you're playing for the first time you have no clue where you need to go, who you need to talk to or what you need to do to find the water chip your vault so desperately needs. Most likely you'll waste a lot of time due to this, time you spend either exploring the wasteland, visiting settlements or interacting with NPCs. By the time you realize that, your vault has almost run out of water so you start making less than ideal decisions. And it is very likely that on the first run you won't manage to deliver the water chip or that you barely do (after all don't forget to account for the time it takes to physically go and deliver the water chip). However if you've played the game a couple times you already have a general sense of what to do, therefore making the time more than enough to actually deliver the water chip and conduct a few other side quests.

This is not the only time critical part of the game, as there is story after delivering the water chip, but I'll refrain to comment on that since I don't like spoilers (even hidden ones as Steam allows).

Now for the game itself. At game start you can create your character or use a pre-built one. Regardless of the chosen option you will still have the ability to customize it to your heart's content before actually starting the game. Customization follows some simple character information (gender, age, name) and the stats: the classical S.P.E.C.I.A.L. (you'll get more information in-game about it), general stats and optional perks. Do note that your overall character attributes have a deep influence in what is available throughout the game as several dialog options and other elements have minimum requirements. It might take a few playthroughs and experimentation until you find a combination of attributes that fits your particular intended play style. The good thing is that in general different mathematical relations between the stats are displayed, so you have a general idea of how to change them to suit your needs.

Combat is turn based on an hexagonal grid where each action consumes Action Points (AP - obviously determined by different stat combinations, among other things). You want to move while in combat mode? AP. You want to access the inventory while in combat mode? AP. Interact with the environment? AP. Aim for a specific body part instead of just shooting at someone randomly? Slightly more AP then just the shooting option. And so on and so forth. Of course that you aren't always in combat mode (although you can always trigger it for various purposes) so don't be afraid - opening doors outside of combat has nothing to do with AP. Combat itself though is highly tied to it (in case you haven't noticed by now) and it affects both you and all of the other participants (each with their own AP limits and consumptions). Speaking of other participants, there does not seem to be an upper bound to how many participants exist in combat at the same time, meaning you can literally have a whole city section in the combat either with or against you. And obviously you have a plethora of gear to fit your needs or areas of expertise (e.g. melee vs firearms).

As for the environment you have several settlements in the wasteland that you can visit, some more friendly than others. Each settlement has different complexities making for a nice variety in the world. Furthermore there are a lot of side quests you can do in each settlement so you're likely to spend some time in each. Other than the settlements you have a big wasteland to explore. Lots of random encounters can happen in the wasteland as well as some other hidden goodies. Do take care as you venture in the wasteland as venturing to a dangerous area under-prepared might mean you cannot double back to a settlement safely. Furthermore, travelling through the wasteland consumes a lot of time, so make sure you have time to spare before going out exploring.

Regarding NPCs there are a big variety of them. They mostly fall under three categories: random NPCs that do not offer much in terms of interaction (you don't even get the dialog interface, they just spout out some random text), NPCs that might have some influence in your stories / information gathering (you have access to the complete dialog interface) and key NPCs that besides the regular dialog interface even have voice-over and a close up of their face that corresponds to their speech. This gives you a very clear distinction when you first approach an NPC of how important they are. Furthermore, through the dialog interface you can access all of the bartering options and a special free text conversation mode. Although to be honest this last feature was never really used by me outside of my first playthrough as most NPCs don't really react to anything you say, so I am not aware of a lot of usages of it.

One thing to note is that there can be some memory / savefile corruption from time to time that might render the game unplayable at specific points, This however is usually gone by loading a previous save file and restarting the quest / area that caused the error. So my recommendation is that you make use of the several save game slots to keep the game saved at different points in time. This way you can load a previous savefile without losing too much progress. My usual rule of thumb is to keep three slots: one for the quick save/load, one before I enter any major area or before/after any (side)quest and a final one for points in time when I make decisions I am not sure I want to make. This way I usually have enough freedom to load earlier savefiles that are not corrupted.

All in all, the game is very coherent and provides a pleasant gaming experience that you'll love if you are a fan of the RPG genre.

Most builds can be viable, but if you don't understand the engine you may unintentionally gimp youirself. Pick something boilerplate that interests you online, and make your own build for your second play through. It's when the game begins to shine.
